sn1.46:1.1: The nymphs (_accharā_, “aquatics”, perhaps originally cloud-deities) were known from Vedic times as beautiful dancers and musicians often romantically entwined with the _gandhabba_.
sn1.46:1.2: As horrifying as nymphs are seductive, the flesh-eating _pisāca_ (Sanskrit _piśāca_) arises in troops under cover of night and slips through the air wreaking havoc.
sn1.46:1.3: Delusion contains both desire and aversion.
sn1.46:2.1: This Sutta contrasts the “direct” way with the “deluding” (_mohana_) way. This recalls the notion that the teaching shows the way to those who are lost (_mūḷhassa vā maggaṁ ācikkheyya_, [sn7.1:9.3]()). This echoes the common description of the Saṅgha as practicing the way that is “direct”, suggesting that they are proceeding directly along a known route ([sn11.3:11.2]()).
sn1.46:2.3: Verses connecting parts of the Dhamma to a chariot are also found at [sn41.5]() and [sn45.4](). | Chariots appear throughout the Vedic literature as vehicles of gods and heroes, and in metaphors especially for the sun and the sacrifice. Rig Veda 10.135.3 speaks of a chariot created by the mind, with a single pole and facing all directions, which connects a grieving son with his departed father.
sn1.46:2.4: Normally _dhammacakka_, the “wheel of the teaching”, is singular, this being a unique plural. The commentary explains as mental and physical energy.
